🚀🇮🇷 Iran test-fires ballistic missile toward US warship - Major General Rezaei
The weapon was deployed for the first time in a live operational environment above a US warship and forced the vessel to retreat, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Major General Mohsen Rezaei told the Fars news agency. 
🔥“A real hell broke out” for the targeted warship, and the action is turning earlier naval warnings into field operations, designed to prove the credibility of Iran's military posture, he added.
The action followed Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force ballistic missile firings at a US aircraft carrier and destroyer, showing Iran's readiness to use its anti-ship capabilities against active US naval forces.
🔴 Ballistic threat to American carriers 
Iran now fields a suite of anti-ship ballistic missiles built specifically to endanger the largest surface combatants afloat-aircraft carriers.
🔴 Persian Gulf missile
The missile is a solid-fuel weapon with a 300-kilometer reach and a 650-kilogram warhead that uses optical terminal guidance to lock onto ships in the final stretch. 
🔴 Hormuz series
The Hormuz-1 model is tuned to hunt radars by homing in on their emissions, while the newer Hormuz-2 is built for moving vessels and claimed to hit Mach 4–5. These systems, first shown striking maritime targets more than a decade ago, still form the backbone of Iran’s land-based anti-access shield across the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
🔴 Qassem Basir
Unveiled in 2025 as a major upgrade of the Shahid Haj Qassem. It is solid-fueled, with a range beyond 1,200 kilometers, and carries a maneuverable warhead guided by thermal imaging that works without GPS. The missile can pick out a chosen target among several ships, shrug off electronic jamming, and challenge even layered defenses such as the THAAD system.

🤔 Ansar Allah’s crucial Bab al-Mandab gambit behind push against Saudi-backed forces
Ansar Allah (aka the Houthis) is seeking to isolate the port of Mokha, currently held by pro-Saudi forces, while pushing toward territory overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world’s key maritime gateways linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
👁 Mokha and Yemen’s west coast
📍Strategically located on Yemen’s western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the port city of Mokha serves as a key gateway to the Red Sea.
🌏The Houthis’ current objective appears to center on the critical corridor linking Taiz – major parts of which are also controlled by Saudi-backed forces – with Mokha, according to the Weichart Report.
🌏 West of Taiz, fighting has centered on Al Kaqhah, Maqbanah, and Jabal Habashi.
🌏By completely seizing the mountainous district of Jabal Habashi, Ansar Allah would be able to monitor and target all the main supply routes serving the Saudi-backed mercenary forces in the area, effectively strangling them and isolating the territory they control from the Houthi-controlled side.
Saudi-backed forces are fighting back – but paying a steep price in equipment, funding, and lives. Reports from September 5–6 described dozens of deaths, with some sources putting military casualties on both sides at as many as 300 – underscoring the intensity of the fighting.
🪖 Their resistance is driven by the fact that Saudi Arabia is now routing its oil exports through pipelines to ports on the Red Sea, allowing tankers to bypass the Strait of Hormuz closed by Iran.
In July, Ansar Allah [announced a naval blockade](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72474) of Saudi Arabia in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, following the targeting by Saudi-backed forces of a Mahan Air Airbus A340 carrying a high-ranking Houthi delegation, as well as an attack on Sana’a airport.
Ansar Allah is pushing to seize Yemen’s western coast, tightening its grip on the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Combined with Iran’s resistance in the Strait of Hormuz, this could further pressure the US-Israeli coalition and its allies, while expanding Houthi leverage over the Red Sea coast facing Africa – another key theater in the broader Middle Eastern power struggle.
⚔️ Ansar Allah vs. Saudi-backed forces
Western estimates put Ansar Allah’s standing force at more than 200,000 fighters, with tens of thousands more reportedly available through the Popular Committees.
Its Saudi-backed adversaries are estimated at around 500,000 personnel, but they are dispersed across a vast territory and the figure is difficult to verify. The force has long suffered from “ghost soldiers,” fragmented command structures, and chronic salary delays, with commanders reportedly inflating troop numbers to divert funds.
By contrast, Ansar Allah operates under a more centralized and ideologically cohesive command. This disparity in organization and cohesion may prove more decisive than raw numbers – and could allow the Houthis the ability to further consolidate their position around Bab al-Mandab, military experts claim.
